RagShortTexts: Mamluk Sultan Qutuz and General Baibars marshaled their slave-soldier corps to face the Mongol.

Variants.Content: In Cairo the Bahri Mamluks, warriors drawn from Kipchak slave stock, held supreme power. Sultan Saif ad-Din Qutuz had put Hulagu's envoys to death and allied with the commander Rukn al-Din Baibars, assembling the most formidable professional army in the Islamic world. The Mamluk regime rested on its military household, whose members were trained from youth, freed, and granted iqta fiefs in return for service. Egypt's wealth came from Nile grain, the Red Sea trade and the taxes of its cities, and that wealth paid for the cavalry, the armourers and the fortresses on which the sultanate's survival depended. Every campaign against the Mongols began with the question of whether the treasury could afford the horses.

The slave-soldiers of Cairo demanded full submission and heavy war taxes from the notables of Egypt. Qutuz had confiscated baronial bullion across the land and declared that any nobleman who withheld coin from the holy defence would lose both fortune and head. Ledgers of every confiscation went to the sultan's treasury, and the men who paid quickly kept their heads.

A Mamluk heavy cavalryman trains relentlessly in the furusiyya, loosing armour-piercing arrows at full gallop before closing with two-handed maces. Hour after hour in the training yard builds the iron discipline that rivals the Mongol tumens. A rider who breaks formation in the line is sent back to the barracks, and the sergeant ends the drill only when every man can strike at speed.
The tax collectors emptied our granaries, but folk along the Nile keep silent. If the Mamluk steel breaks in Syria, the riders who slaughtered Baghdad will drink our water and burn our fields.
